Ever wondered what neural networks are and how they work? 

Systems like ChatGPT use neural networks to work as well as they do.  Neural networks are composed of neurons that make up layers, layers with different functions, connections between the layers called weights, and mathematical functions called activation functions. If youâre interested in learning about these systems more deeply, I have a series called the 10 Days of AI Basics that goes in depth â comment LEARN and Iâll send it to you. 

Ultimately, the neural network structure of the model is a way of visualizing how the model is actually just a complex mathematical equation. When companies release the weights of the model, they are releasing a key piece that is needed to run the full equation of the model. Without the weights, the equation is incomplete.

For the math-minded: the weights of a model are the learned numbers (they are variables during training) that are then used as constants in the mathematical functions that make up the model. Neural networks are ultimately, just one big, hyper-complex mathematical function, and when a model is trained, it is learning the constants associated with the high-dimensional variable input.

First recorded by Allan Fakir for Radio Pakistan in the late 1970s, 'Tarrin Paunda' (or Ti Pawanda Tarien) is one of the most ethereal & sublime songs in the vast repository of Sindh's ancient Sufi folk lore.

Famed for his ecstatic performances, eccentric body language, enchanting expressions & extreme devotional singing coupled with Sufi dance, Allan Fakir was the impeccable & preeminent harbinger of Sindhi Sufi music in Pakistan.

Notwithstanding his father's disdain for his penchant for singing, Allan persevered, singing melancholic Sufi songs. He mastered the art of expressing the poetic mysticism of the ancient Sufi saints who had once settled along the River Indus in what is now the arid province of Sindh, Pakistan.

In 1950, as a mutinous youth, Allan sundered all bonds with his father. Wholly bereft of a mother's love, he sought someone who could replace that love. He found solace at the shrine of Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai in Bhit Shah. Although unlettered, Fakir had an extraordinary memory. Hearing the traditional Latifi Raag sung every night touched his heart & stirred his soul. 

Encouraged by Faqir Zawar Qurban Ali Lanjwani & Moolchand Maharaj, Fakir began singing Bhitaiâs poetry at the shrine, spending 20 years in devotion before being introduced to Radio Pakistan & PTV by Mumtaz Mirza, and ultimately becoming an eminent luminary.

'Tarrin Paunda' is often erroneously ascribed to the 18th-century Sufi saint, Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, but it was actually penned by Shaikh Ayaz. As a Marxist in his youth, Ayaz later became a trusted confidant of the acclaimed Sindhi scholar GM Syed, with whom he later had a falling out in the 1980s.

Ayazâs most prolific & fecund period of writing spanned from the early 1960s to the late 1970s, during which he composed 'Tarrin Paunda' in the 1970s. Ayaz drew inspiration from the mesmerizing poetic cadence of Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai's oeuvres.

The song is about a manâs urge to one day meet his beloved when his natural surroundings will be in full bloom. The poem was penned by Ayaz to be sung hypnotically, ensnaring the singer in an eternal cycle of hope, despair, love & melancholy. Allan Fakir achieved that perfectly!
